opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's really one of the things that's changed most for us over the last couple of years. Historically, when you went into a new city, there was a sense that you had to do a lot of bespoke work: collect a lot of data locally, find the long tail of situations that were specific to that place, tune things, validate extensively, and only then expand. And some of that is still necessary. Safety validation in a new environment is not something you skip.

But what we've seen is that as our models get larger, are trained on more diverse data, and especially as we lean on these more general learned representations, a lot of what used to look like city-specific problems turn out to be instances of things the model has already seen in some form. A tricky unprotected left in one city isn't fundamentally that different from one somewhere else. The road users, the dynamics, the intent of other agents. A lot of that transfers. So the amount of new learning you need in a new market shrinks quite a bit.

Practically, that means the process shifts from "teach the driver this city" to "verify that the driver already handles this city, and find the residual gaps." You still drive there, you still collect data, but much of that effort goes into evaluation, into looking for the genuinely novel things: maybe different road markings, local driving norms, weather like snow, or infrastructure we haven't seen much of. Then you address those in a targeted way, and ideally that improvement flows back into the general model and makes every city better, not just the new one.

The other piece is simulation. With stronger generative and behavior models, we can build realistic scenarios for a new environment and stress-test the driver before and alongside real-world operation. That lets us find issues faster and with more coverage than relying purely on miles driven.

So the net effect is that expansion gets faster and more scalable, but the bar doesn't move. The generalization buys you speed in getting to the point where you can demonstrate safety, and that's really what lets us think about going to many more cities, including internationally, in a much more systematic way than was possible before.

r001.rationale: The response mentions market-specific differences and residual gaps, but does not state that markets more different from existing ones place greater demands on model generalization.

r002.rationale: It says stronger generalization reduces new-market learning and speeds reaching the point where Waymo can demonstrate safety, while safety validation remains required.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's really central to how we think about scaling the business. So let me give you a bit of context first.

Historically, when you brought an autonomous driving system to a new city, it was a pretty involved process. You'd map the area in detail, you'd collect a lot of data locally, you'd identify the new behaviors, the new road geometries, the local driving culture, the weather, and then you'd iterate on the system until it handled all of that well. Phoenix is very different from San Francisco, and San Francisco is very different from Los Angeles or Austin. So in the early days, each new city was almost its own project.

What we've seen over the last few years, and this is really a story about the models, is that as we've moved to larger, more end-to-end learned components, and as we've trained them on a much broader and more diverse set of driving data, the system generalizes a lot better out of the box. When we take the Waymo Driver to a new place, a lot of it just works. The things that were specific to one city become, in effect, part of a much larger distribution the model has already seen. And so the amount of city-specific work shrinks quite a bit.

Concretely, the way that changes the process is a few things. One, the validation burden shifts. Instead of finding and fixing a long tail of local issues, we're spending more of our effort confirming that the behavior we expect is actually there, and looking for the genuinely novel cases, which are fewer. Two, our tooling for evaluation becomes more important than our tooling for hand-tuning. We lean heavily on simulation and on our ability to measure performance against our safety framework, and that infrastructure transfers very well between cities. And three, it makes the data flywheel more effective: every new city we enter adds diversity to the training set, which in turn makes the next city easier.

I'd add a caveat, which is that generalization doesn't mean zero local work. There are still things like local regulations, specific operational considerations, interactions with first responders, and so on, that we'll always do carefully with each community. And we still do a lot of driving in a new city before we open to the public, because safety is the bar and we need evidence, not just confidence in the model. But the trend is clear. We went from one city to, you know, several in a fairly short period of time, and the models generalizing better is a big part of why that pace is possible. I expect that to continue as the models keep improving.

r001.rationale: The response notes that cities differ and says the model generalizes better across them, but it does not state that entering markets more different from existing ones places greater demands on generalization.

r002.rationale: It says improved generalization reduces city-specific work and novel issues, shifting effort toward validation, and identifies better generalization as a reason Waymo can expand at a faster pace while still gathering safety evidence.

astra-6.text:
Stronger generalization means that less of the work has to be specific to each new city. You want the system to learn principles of driving that transfer—how to interact with other road users, how to understand an unfamiliar intersection—rather than depend on having seen a particular situation in a particular place.

So, as that improves, bringing Waymo into a new market becomes less about adapting the model to every local variation. The experience we gain in one market can help us drive better in another, and that can make expansion more efficient.

But generalization doesn’t remove the need for validation. A new market may have different road layouts, driving behaviors, or weather conditions. We still need to understand those differences and establish that the system handles them safely. The opportunity is to have more of that capability transfer from the start, so the remaining work is focused on the differences that actually matter.

r001.rationale: The response mentions that new markets may differ in layouts, behaviors, and weather, but does not say that greater differences place greater demands on model generalization.

r002.rationale: It says stronger generalization can make market expansion more efficient and separately says safety validation remains necessary, but does not clearly state that generalization accelerates the process of establishing safety in a new market.

sol-6.1.text:
I think stronger generalization really changes how much work you need to do for each new city. You want the system to learn principles of driving that transfer, so that when you encounter a different road layout or a slightly different traffic pattern, you’re not starting from scratch.

There will still be local differences, and you need to understand those and validate that the system handles them safely. But as the models get better at transferring what they’ve learned, entering a new market becomes less about developing new behaviors and more about evaluating where the system is already capable and addressing the remaining gaps. That gives us a path to expanding more efficiently while maintaining a high safety bar.

r001.rationale: The response says generalization helps handle different road layouts and traffic patterns, but does not state that markets farther from existing ones place greater demands on generalization.

r002.rationale: It says stronger transfer means less new behavior development and more efficient market entry, while still validating local differences for safety.
